domain: International Law / Maritime Governance / Geopolitical Strategy
topic_summary: Analysis of contested interpretations of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), focusing on conflicts between strict exclusive economic zone (EEZ) enforcement and expansive historical rights claims. The substrate is UNCLOS itself as a founding legal kernel; different state readings produce structurally incompatible sovereignty and resource control regimes.

key_entities: UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea - founding legal kernel)
Coastal States (primary beneficiaries of EEZ regime)
China (expansive historical rights claimant via nine-dash line)
United States (non-ratifier enforcing freedom of navigation)
International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS - interpretive authority)
key_tensions: EEZ exclusivity vs historical rights overlay (strict reading vs expansive reading)
Ratifier obligations vs non-ratifier enforcement (U.S. enforces rules it hasn't ratified)
Resource sovereignty vs navigational freedom (coastal control vs maritime commons)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: UNCLOS as codified maritime law establishing EEZ boundaries, territorial waters, and resource rights - the stabilized international legal framework for ocean governance
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) plus domestic courts of ratifying states; legitimacy grounded in treaty ratification and customary international law status
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Contested Legitimacy Pattern - multiple authorities claim interpretive primacy over the same kernel with incompatible readings

readings.commitment: EEZ boundaries are exclusive and enforceable per UNCLOS Article 57 200-nautical-mile limits; no overlay claims valid
readings.authority_grounding: ITLOS rulings (e.g., Philippines v. China 2016) plus majority coastal state practice
readings.expected_structural_delta: Coastal states enter beneficiary set with exclusive resource control; overlapping claimants enter victim set (lose access); high suppression of alternative sovereignty frameworks

readings.commitment: Historical usage and occupation create sovereign rights that predate and override UNCLOS EEZ provisions
readings.authority_grounding: Domestic legal frameworks of claimant states (e.g., China's 1992 Territorial Sea Law); rejection of ITLOS authority as Western-imposed
readings.expected_structural_delta: Expansive claimant states enter beneficiary set; EEZ-holding coastal states enter victim set (lose exclusive control); navigational actors face constraint increase

readings.commitment: Freedom of navigation principles are customary international law independent of UNCLOS ratification; enforceable by naval presence
readings.authority_grounding: U.S. military doctrine plus other major naval powers; legitimacy grounded in customary law and power projection capacity
readings.expected_structural_delta: Naval powers enter beneficiary set (enforce rules without treaty obligations); coastal states attempting EEZ exclusivity enter victim set; constraint structure decouples from legal text

axiom_contradictions.basis: One holds that EEZ boundaries are legally exclusive and override prior claims; the other holds that historical sovereignty preexists and supersedes treaty-created boundaries. No single coherent framework can hold both - accepting historical rights as valid requires rejecting EEZ exclusivity, and vice versa.

One grounds maritime law authority in ratified treaty text with tribunal adjudication; the other decouples enforcement from treaty membership via customary law claims. A framework cannot simultaneously hold that UNCLOS authority derives from ratification AND that non-ratifiers can enforce its provisions through military power.
